title: House Adopts Flick’s Resolution Recognizing Little League World Series Week
raw_text:
House Adopts Flick’s Resolution Recognizing Little League World Series Week
June 30, 2026
HARRISBURG – Recognizing its cherished tradition and the significant impact it has on the Commonwealth, Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) announced Aug. 19-30, 2026, will be recognized as “Little League World Series Week” in Pennsylvania. The designation follows the successful passage of a resolution he sponsored, which was approved by an overwhelming majority in the House of Representatives.
House Resolution 554
honors the Little League World Series, which is held each year in South Williamsport, the birthplace of Little League. It also recognizes Carl E. Stotz, who founded Little League in 1939.
“I’m proud to pay tribute to Carl, whose vision and dedication gave rise to Little League and helped shape generations of young athletes,” Flick said. “This resolution is an opportunity to celebrate the value of teamwork, sportsmanship and community that continue to define the Little League World Series and our region.”
Each year tens of thousands of visitors from around the world travel to South Williamsport for the Little League World Series. It’s estimated the event bring in $40 million to the economy as teams from Canada to Cuba, Texas to Taiwan, and Pennsylvania to Puerto Rico compete to become world champions.
Flick, who has not missed a Little League World Series tournament for more than 50 years, serves as a team host and hosts an annual picnic for two of the participating teams.
“This resolution ensures we continue to honor the history and values Little League represents,” Flick said. “I’m looking forward to this year’s World Series and to welcoming the young athletes and families who make this event so special.”
In speaking on the House floor in support of his resolution, Flick paid tribute to Karen Stotz Myers, the daughter of Stotz, who remains an active advocate for preserving and recognizing the league’s original field about five miles from where the World Series is played today. He also recognized Billy Martin of Houston, Texas., who threw the first no-hitter in the 1950 Little League World Series and continues to return to the tournament.

title: Decision Shaped by Open Debate and Informed Discussions, Not Party Lines
raw_text:
Decision Shaped by Open Debate and Informed Discussions, Not Party Lines
June 2, 2026
by State Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union)
Laws are created for many reasons: for protection, regulation, to promote fairness and safety, establish consistency, resolve conflicts, and enable trust. When legislators vote, we are responsible for educating ourselves and being open to hearing both sides of an issue.
At times, I can vote on a bill with firm conviction. Other times I listen to arguments for and against and find myself changing my mind with each new speaker. What will be best for everyone in the long run? This was the case with House Bill 1814, which passed in the House on June 1.
House Bill 1814
would ban the possession and use of cell phones and other mobile devices by students in K–12 during school hours in both public and private learning environments across the Commonwealth, with certain exemptions included in the legislation.
My instinct was to vote ‘yes.’ I believe cell phone use is hindering education in classrooms, with students of all ages distracted by whatever content is more interesting than the subject at hand. As a grown adult, I find myself distracted, drawn to my phone to learn, to be entertained or to follow whatever discussion is taking over social media. My initial “yes” was based on the belief that it would take a law to rein in cell phone usage in schools.
Then I thought about my belief in small government, and not making sweeping laws to govern every inch of this diverse Commonwealth with one stroke of a pen. School districts elect people to make policies that fit their educational needs, isn’t that the role of a school board? My vote then swung to “no.”
Then I thought about how local elections can sometimes go awry if the candidates elected are not qualified or willing to listen to and act on the best interest of their constituents. I think of Muncy Township and the swelling discontent with the chairperson of that board of supervisors. Is it sometimes better to pass laws to govern from the top? Maybe I should vote “yes.”
I listened to the arguments made in the House chamber, both for and against, and then I made some phone calls to local superintendents and to a handful of school board presidents. We talked about the issue.
Around 420 of 500 school districts in the Commonwealth already have a cell phone policy in place. Here in the 83rd District, schools have differing policies that seem to be working well for them. Making these decisions is what local elected officials, school board directors, are elected to do. I voted “no.”
House Bill 1814 does not resolve all conflicts, build trust or promote fairness regarding the autonomy school districts need to meet the needs of students, teachers and administrators.
The House ultimately passed the bill by a vote of 126 to 75. Support and opposition to the bill came from both parties. This was not a vote divided by party, but by educated differences of opinion, and that’s how it is supposed to work.
House Bill 1814 now heads to the Senate, which has already passed a similar bill. Senate members will consider the amendments the House made to the bill before making their final vote.

title: House Approves Flick’s Resolution Honoring Negro Leagues

House Approves Flick’s Resolution Honoring Negro Leagues
May 4, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) announced May 2, 2026, is now Negro Leagues Day in Pennsylvania. The designation follows the successful passage of a resolution he sponsored, which was approved on Monday by an overwhelming majority in the House of Representatives.
House Resolution 481
recognizes the contributions African American baseball players made to the game and acknowledges the significant impact the Negro Leagues had on the civil rights movement nationwide.
“In 1865, one of the first Negro baseball clubs was formed in Philadelphia, the Philadelphia Phythians,” Flick said. “For over a century and a half, Pennsylvania has been a shining example of how sports, specifically baseball, can be a place of inclusion. This resolution ensures that legacy is honored and the stories of these groundbreaking players continue to be shared.”
Flick, an avid baseball fan, belongs to the Williamsport chapter of the Society for American Baseball Research (SABR). This chapter is known as the George Stovey chapter. Stovey, who was born and lived in Williamsport, is widely recognized as one of the best left-handed pitchers of the 19th century, but unfortunately, because of the color of his skin, he was not allowed to play in the major leagues.
Flick credits SABR members in the Williamsport, Harrisburg and Philadelphia chapters for suggesting the idea of the resolution. He said he wants to ensure players like Stovey receive the recognition they were long denied.
“Baseball is America’s pastime, and I think it’s past time George Stovey and great players like him are recognized,” Flick said. “Without proper recognition, Stovey and so many players like him have been left out of the Baseball Hall of Fame.”

Looking Back on the 79th Little League World Series
September 2, 2026
by State Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union)
Now that the Little League World Series (LLWS) has come and gone I wanted to take a moment to recognize some of the special moments. We can agree that some of the highlights this year include Curaçao’s pitching domination in the final game, Japan’s heartfelt celebration after winning their final matchup with help from their smallest player. There was also the record-setting play of both “girls with game,” Kinley Rasmus of Phenix City, Alabama, and Carsynn Meyer of Paseo Verde Little League in Las Vegas, Nevada.
One of my favorite moments of the series didn’t even occur on the diamond, but on the slick, muddy hill. I watched the kids slide down, run back up, and slide back down; a frenzy of kids caked in mud having fun. But when the speakers began to play a national anthem, whether it was the Star-Spangled Banner or another country’s anthem, they stopped in deference to the tradition. I was proud to witness such respect, and it affirms that, yes, the kids are alright.
This year I volunteered as Team Host for Team Canada, and I saw and experienced kindness, respect, great sportsmanship, and commendable behavior in the Canadians and all the teams who came to play on our fields. I’m left feeling encouraged and hopeful.
I also want to congratulate the brave and determined players of the Challenger Exhibition game held on Saturday. It is possibly the most joyful game of the Series, when the kids who face physical and developmental challenges take to the field, swing the bat and run the bases. This year’s teams hailed from Berwyn/Paoli, Pennsylvania, and Oakley, California. Before the players met at Volunteer Stadium, they practiced at the Original Little League Field in Williamsport, and they participated in a program called Drums Alive with the Superstars group at the Williamsport YMCA. Many thanks to the Superstars, the Williamsport YMCA, BLaST IU17, Park Pizza for donating pizzas to both teams, PepsiCo, and especially the families for supporting their kids on the long journey to Williamsport.
Lastly, I want to take a moment to congratulate all of us, as fans and as hosts. The Little League World Series is our time to show the world that North Central Pennsylvania, the 83rd District, South Williamsport, Williamsport, and the surrounding communities are great places to live, populated with good and welcoming people. $100,000 Grant Given to Williamsport for Housing Needs, Says Flick
September 1, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) announced the City of Williamsport will receive $100,000 to help address the city’s housing concerns. The city was granted the money through the state’s Municipal Assistance Program (MAP).
The funding will go to the creation of a housing needs assessment and action plan. The proposed plan will analyze existing housing conditions and provide an action plan to address identified concerns. To develop the plan, the City of Williamsport will partner with the City of Williamsport Redevelopment and Land Bank Authority.
“Access to safe, affordable and quality housing is critical to any community,” Flick said. “This funding will help Williamsport better understand its current and future housing needs and develop a plan to address the challenges facing residents and neighborhoods across the city. As the state representative for the region, I look forward to reviewing the study’s findings and supporting the efforts that will strengthen Williamsport’s neighborhoods.
Valerie Fessler, director of Community and Economic Development for the City of Williamsport, echoed similar sentiments.
“This housing study will give the city a better understanding of our current housing needs, identify gaps and opportunities, and help us develop a strategic approach to expanding and improving our housing stock,” Fessler said. “We are extremely grateful to the Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development for recognizing the importance of this work and for supporting Williamsport through the MAP grant program. This partnership will provide us with valuable data and a roadmap to make informed decisions and pursue future investments that will strengthen our neighborhoods and benefit residents throughout our community.”
Through MAP, municipalities and counties may apply for grant funding to cover up to 50% of eligible costs related to community planning and shared services.
Representative Jamie Flick
83rd District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

Give Me Your Feedback on Proposed Department of Health Regulations
Recently, the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) proposed updates to regulations on communicable diseases. These proposals have been submitted to the Independent Regulatory Review Commission (IRRC) for review under Rulemaking #10-242: Communicable and Noncommunicable Disease.
The policies being reviewed for updates are used to establish the formal rules that govern how communicable diseases are reported and managed, and they must undergo IRRC review before becoming final.
This is getting a lot of attention, as the proposed updates are comparable to similar measures used during the COVID-19 pandemic. As written, the DOH proposals would permit state officials to implement school or community mask requirements, conduct certain inspections or interviews as part of disease investigation activities, and request health information for contact-tracing or related public-health purposes. It also includes provisions allowing officials to enter school buildings to interview students privately for disease-control efforts.

More Than $2 Million in LSA Funding Supports Community Projects in Lycoming, Union Counties, Says Flick
September 15, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) today highlighted his work to bring in more than $750,000 in Local Share Account (LSA) grants to parts of Lycoming and Union counties. Flick also announced an additional nearly $1.25 million of the same funding to further support community projects throughout the region.
The funding was approved by the Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA).
Local Share Account grants are funded through gaming revenues under Act 71 of 2004 and are used to support economic development, community improvement and public interest projects.
“I’m glad to see this significant funding coming to municipalities across Lycoming and Union counties,” Flick said. “These dollars will support job training and provide local governments with the infrastructure and equipment they need to continue delivering essential services.”

•
Loyalsock Township - $246,381
to purchase a bucket truck.
•
Montgomery Borough - $174,352,
on behalf of Montgomery Volunteer Fire Department, to replace radios.
•
South Williamsport Borough - $250,000
to make road improvements and infrastructure improvements in the borough.
•
White Deer Township - $92,147
to replace playground equipment at West Milton Memorial Park.
Funding secured jointly with Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Bradford/Lycoming/Sullivan/Tioga/Union):
•
Gregg Township Municipal Authority - $400,000
for a sewer line rehabilitation project in Gregg Township, Union County, and Brady Township, Lycoming County.
•
Lycoming County - $247,000
, on behalf of Pennsylvania College of Technology, to purchase new equipment for its Aviation and Heavy Equipment Operations degree programs.
Other funding approved includes:
•
Economic and Community Growth Corporation of Lycoming County - $400,000
on behalf of Lycoming College to build a new baseball stadium.
•
Williamsport City - $200,000
for a new storage facility for the police department.
The Commonwealth Financing Authority is an independent agency responsible for administering state investments that support Pennsylvania’s economic growth and community development.

title: Flick Announces Oct. 5 Press Conference, Hearing and Panel at State Capitol for Child Custody Reform Legislation
raw_text:
Flick Announces Oct. 5 Press Conference, Hearing and Panel at State Capitol for Child Custody Reform Legislation
September 28, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) today announced there will be a major day for his child custody reform legislation as there is a press conference, Judiciary Committee public hearing and panel all scheduled for Monday, Oct. 5, at the State Capitol in Harrisburg.
All the events will focus on
House Bill 1499
, authored by Flick, which would ensure fairness in custody determinations and protect the rights of children to have equal access to both parents, provided they are willing, able and fit.
“Momentum has been building for House Bill 1499,” Flick said. “I’m excited we’ve reached this point as I continue to hear from fathers, mothers and grandparents from across the country who share their own experiences about the need for reform. I encourage supporters of the legislation to come to Harrisburg if they can participate in this important day.”
A press conference will take place at 9 a.m. on the steps of the Main Capitol Rotunda. Speakers at the press conference will include Flick; Robert Garza, director for Americans for Judicial Accountability and a nationally recognized advocate for children and parental rights; Mark Ludwig, executive director of the National Council for Equal Shared Parenting; Jeff Steiner, M.Ed., executive director of Dads’ Resource Center; Hon. Mica Wood Pence, 43rd Circuit judge from Barren and Metcalfe counties in Kentucky, the first state to enact an equal parenting law; Hon. Tony Payton, former member, Pennsylvania House of Representatives; Teresa Sneed, founder, president and chief executive officer, National Family Justice; Rael LaPenta, a member of Mothers Against Child Abuse; and several other advocates of child custody reform.
“I am thrilled to have so many people who believe in the need for reform coming together at the Capitol,” Flick said. “House Bill 1499 has 78 co-sponsors from both parties and a grassroots petition that has gathered more than 2,800 signatures. This bill is really a child-focused bill as it considers the best interest of children when it comes to both safety and emotional wellbeing.”
Flick is also going to be part of a House Judiciary Committee public hearing at 10 a.m. in the Majority Caucus Room (140 Main Capitol) which will center on House Bill 1499.
“House Bill 1499 has been lingering in the Judiciary Committee since May 2025 despite having undeniable support,” Flick said. “This is a momentous opportunity to bring this issue before the committee.”
Flick will also be hosting a public House Bill 1499 Panel from 12:30 – 2 p.m. in Room B-31 Main Capitol. The panel will serve as an opportunity to hear directly from parents, grandparents and others who have been directly impacted by Pennsylvania’s current custody system within the framework of "why House Bill 1499 is important to me."
“I want to give as many people as possible the chance to be heard,” Flick said. “The panel will be a very public way to share the stories from parents who have lost access to their children at the whim of a judge or on a false allegation. My bill calls for 50/50 custody from the start for willing, able and fit parents, with a clear path for a modified custody agreement when clear and convincing evidence shows custody should not be 50/50.”
Pennsylvania has previously taken steps toward child custody reform. Last year, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed House Bill 378 into law as Act 11 of 2025. This bill reduces the factors a judge considers during child custody cases from 19 to 12. Flick wrote an amendment to the bill, which was unanimously passed by the House, requiring the court to give everyone a copy of the new factors within 30 days of modifications being made so that every party, including parents who often represent themselves because hiring lawyers is so expensive, has fair access to information.
“Act 11 of 2025 is working," Flick said. "In multiple cases, the Pennsylvania Superior Court has vacated and remanded lower court custody modifications because of a judge's failure to review the streamlined custody factors or provide written justifications in a timely manner as state law now mandates."
Flick was also a co-sponsor of  House Bill 414, now Act 40 of 2025, known as the Uniform Deployed Parents Custody and Visitation Act, which prohibits permanent custody changes during a parent’s military deployment. Shapiro signed the legislation into law at the end of October, which fixes a major flaw in the child custody system that allowed parents to use deployment as a reason to alter existing custody arrangements.
On Nov. 18, 2025 Flick also hosted another major day for shared parenting reform. A highlight from the day included a Republican Policy Committee hearing, where testifiers included Teresa Sneed, founder, president and chief executive officer, National Family Justice; Hon. Tony Payton, former member, Pennsylvania House of Representatives; Greg Fellerman, founding partner, Fellerman and Ciarimboli Law; and Hon. Mica Wood Pence.
Seven other states - Kentucky, Arkansas, West Virginia, Florida, Missouri, Louisiana and Mississippi - have passed or adopted similar child custody legislation.
“Pennsylvania can, and should, be a leader in child custody,” Flick said. “Without shared parenting, children are more likely to struggle in school, face emotional challenges and fall into cycles that hurt their future.”
Flick welcomes all who are able to attend the events on Oct. 5. For those who can’t attend, he will be streaming the events on his Facebook page and his website, www.RepFlick.com.

title: Flick’s Shared Parenting Legislation Highlighted During Hearing, Press Conference and Panel
raw_text:
Flick’s Shared Parenting Legislation Highlighted During Hearing, Press Conference and Panel
October 5, 2026
HARRISBURG – On Monday, Oct. 5, Rep. Jamie Flick (R Lycoming/Union) hosted another significant day for child custody reform in Pennsylvania. His bill,
House Bill 1499
, which seeks to ensure fairness in custody determinations and protect children’s rights to have equal access to both parents, provided they are willing, fit and able, was the focus of a press conference, Judiciary Committee public hearing and panel at the state Capitol in Harrisburg.
Flick was joined by a large group of legislators, supporters, legal experts, family advocates, parents, grandparents and former lawmakers who support his bill.
“The message in the bill is that kids need both safe, fit and loving parents,” Flick said. “I continue to fight for this important piece of family legislation because every day I get calls from fathers, mothers and grandparents from across the country who share their own experiences about the need for reform.”
Following a morning press conference, the focus shifted to a House Judiciary Committee public hearing where House Bill 1499 was the central issue for discussion. House Bill 1499 has been held without action in the Judiciary Committee since May 2025, despite it having 78 co-sponsors from both parties and a grassroots petition that has gathered more than 2,800 signatures.
The hearing, which lasted more than two hours, was packed with more than 100 supporters of House Bill 1499, who frequently applauded those who supported the bill.
During the hearing, Hon. Mica Wood Pence, 43rd Circuit judge from Barren and Metcalfe counties in Kentucky, the first state to enact an equal parenting law in 2018, offered testimony that she has seen more parents working together and making the best decisions for their children.
“A child should not have one house they live in and one house they visit,” Pence said. “No one wants these children to be abused. One of the things I’m most proud to see in Kentucky is that our rates of abuse have dropped. It’s because a child has two trusted adults they can go to.”
Objection came in from seven of eight panelists who were brought in to oppose Flick’s House Bill 1499 during the House Judiciary Committee’s public hearing. The concerns focused on domestic violence, a presumption of 50/50 at the start of custody determinations, and whether or not House Bill 1499 considers the recently passed Act 11 of 2025 which reduces factors from 19 to 12 when judges are determining custody.
“These factors were passed after House Bill 1499 was drafted,” said Flick. “We did address those factors in a recent amendment.”
Rep. Rob Kauffman, (R-Franklin), Republican chair of the House Judiciary Committee and a co-sponsor of House Bill 1499, said he has been looking for data on how many parents, male or female, are awarded primary custody.
He also acknowledged the concerns about the custody factors and said that while legislation may require judges to be impartial, he has heard anecdotal reports that some judges are not.
Rep. Andrew Kuzma (R-Allegheny/Washington), another co-sponsor of House Bill 1499, and an orphan’s court attorney, said he’s done his own research and found that fathers all across the Commonwealth only receive primary custody 14% of the time.
Rep. Charity Grimm Krupa (R-Fayette), an attorney, said she quit doing custody cases because there was no justice in it.
Reps. Brenda Pugh (R-Luzerne) and George Margetas (R-York), both co-sponsors of House Bill 1499, questioned testifiers and received loud applause when speaking.
“If we are going to presume that custody will be a 50/50 split, why don’t we record it on paper?” Pugh questioned. “Things like drug abuse, child abuse or a Protection from Abuse (PFA) will certainly move the 50/50 custody equation.”
Rep. Margetas said that too often parents in custody cases are at the mercy of the judge they are assigned and must rely on the individual judge’s discretion when determining custody factors.
“We allow criminals to be presumed not guilty until proven guilty,” Margetas said. “Why shouldn’t two good parents have that same presumption unless proven otherwise? Why should litigants across Pennsylvania have to play Russian roulette?”
Prior to the hearing, the day started with a press conference held on the steps of the Main Capitol Rotunda. Flick lead a message of equality for families where supporters held signs that read “Kids Need Both” and “House Bill 1499 Fairness for Families.”
“We are here for the kids,” Flick said. “We are here for Pennsylvania kids.”
Jeff Steiner, M.Ed., executive director of Dads’ Resource Center, offered stories of parents and grandparents who have been isolated from their children and grandchildren through unfair custody hearings. He said it’s frustrating for those who have been waiting since Rep. Flick introduced the bill on May 28, 2025, which he cited as 495 days, for something to happen.
“The support for House Bill 1499 demonstrates that shared parenting is not a partisan issue, because it’s about doing better for Pennsylvania children,” Steiner said. “Pennsylvanians overwhelmingly believe children should have the meaningful involvement of both parents following separation, and we now have an extraordinary bipartisan coalition of legislators willing to seriously examine how we can better serve these families.”
Robert Garza, director for Americans for Judicial Accountability and a nationally recognized advocate for children and parental rights, said he will continue urge parents to fight for 50/50 shared custody.
“This is about protecting the everyday moments that build relationships,” Garza said. “Moments no court can give back once they’re gone. I’m grateful to Rep. Flick for championing this effort.”
Mark Ludwig, executive director of the National Council for Equal Shared Parenting, spoke at the press conference. He has played a key role in advancing similar legislation in several states, including Kentucky, Arkansas, West Virginia, Florida and Missouri.
“Children should not lose a meaningful relationship with either parent simply because their parents no longer live together,” Ludwig said. “I’m proud to stand with Rep. Flick and Pennsylvania families in support of House Bill 1499. When both parents are willing, fit and able children deserve the opportunity to have both fully involved in their lives.”
Rael LaPenta, a member of Mothers Against Child Abuse, a national organization dedicated to protecting children from emotional, psychological, coercive and other forms of maltreatment, said the bill is in the best interest of parents and children.
“I’m a mother of both a son and a daughter,” LaPenta said. “This is not mothers versus fathers. It is about giving our children the safest, healthiest foundation possible. Pennsylvania has already done the studying and made the findings. Now we have the opportunity to act on them. I cannot look at my son and my daughter, and someday perhaps their children, and accept a system that still begins with assumptions instead of evidence. If we believe a child’s emotional and psychological well-being matters, and if Pennsylvania has already recognized the value of safe, meaningful relationships with both parents, then our custody laws should reflect it.”
Flick also took questions and listened to stories during a personal question-and-answer session where people from all over the Commonwealth shared their frustrations and hopes for reform.
“Pennsylvania can, and should, be a leader in child custody,” Flick said. “Without shared parenting, children are more likely to struggle in school, face emotional challenges and fall into cycles that hurt their future. I’m grateful for a day like this where we hear from families impacted by the corrupt child custody system, listen to experts who understand these issues and discuss how we can move this legislation forward to provide greater stability for children and families.”

title: Flick’s Shared Parenting Legislation Highlighted During Hearing, Press Conference and Panel

Flick’s Shared Parenting Legislation Highlighted During Hearing, Press Conference and Panel
October 5, 2026
HARRISBURG – On Monday, Oct. 5, Rep. Jamie Flick (R Lycoming/Union) hosted another significant day for child custody reform in Pennsylvania. His bill,
House Bill 1499
, which seeks to ensure fairness in custody determinations and protect children’s rights to have equal access to both parents, provided they are willing, fit and able, was the focus of a press conference, Judiciary Committee public hearing and panel at the state Capitol in Harrisburg.
Flick was joined by a large group of legislators, supporters, legal experts, family advocates, parents, grandparents and former lawmakers who support his bill.
“The message in the bill is that kids need both safe, fit and loving parents,” Flick said. “I continue to fight for this important piece of family legislation because every day I get calls from fathers, mothers and grandparents from across the country who share their own experiences about the need for reform.”
Following a morning press conference, the focus shifted to a House Judiciary Committee public hearing where House Bill 1499 was the central issue for discussion. House Bill 1499 has been held without action in the Judiciary Committee since May 2025, despite it having 78 co-sponsors from both parties and a grassroots petition that has gathered more than 2,800 signatures.
The hearing, which lasted more than two hours, was packed with more than 100 supporters of House Bill 1499, who frequently applauded those who supported the bill.
During the hearing, Hon. Mica Wood Pence, 43rd Circuit judge from Barren and Metcalfe counties in Kentucky, the first state to enact an equal parenting law in 2018, offered testimony that she has seen more parents working together and making the best decisions for their children.
“A child should not have one house they live in and one house they visit,” Pence said. “No one wants these children to be abused. One of the things I’m most proud to see in Kentucky is that our rates of abuse have dropped. It’s because a child has two trusted adults they can go to.”
Objection came in from seven of eight panelists who were brought in to oppose Flick’s House Bill 1499 during the House Judiciary Committee’s public hearing. The concerns focused on domestic violence, a presumption of 50/50 at the start of custody determinations, and whether or not House Bill 1499 considers the recently passed Act 11 of 2025 which reduces factors from 19 to 12 when judges are determining custody.
“These factors were passed after House Bill 1499 was drafted,” said Flick. “We did address those factors in a recent amendment.”
Rep. Rob Kauffman, (R-Franklin), Republican chair of the House Judiciary Committee and a co-sponsor of House Bill 1499, said he has been looking for data on how many parents, male or female, are awarded primary custody.
He also acknowledged the concerns about the custody factors and said that while legislation may require judges to be impartial, he has heard anecdotal reports that some judges are not.
Rep. Andrew Kuzma (R-Allegheny/Washington), another co-sponsor of House Bill 1499, and an orphan’s court attorney, said he’s done his own research and found that fathers all across the Commonwealth only receive primary custody 14% of the time.
Rep. Charity Grimm Krupa (R-Fayette), an attorney, said she quit doing custody cases because there was no justice in it.
Reps. Brenda Pugh (R-Luzerne) and George Margetas (R-York), both co-sponsors of House Bill 1499, questioned testifiers and received loud applause when speaking.
“If we are going to presume that custody will be a 50/50 split, why don’t we record it on paper?” Pugh questioned. “Things like drug abuse, child abuse or a Protection from Abuse (PFA) will certainly move the 50/50 custody equation.”
Rep. Margetas said that too often parents in custody cases are at the mercy of the judge they are assigned and must rely on the individual judge’s discretion when determining custody factors.
“We allow criminals to be presumed not guilty until proven guilty,” Margetas said. “Why shouldn’t two good parents have that same presumption unless proven otherwise? Why should litigants across Pennsylvania have to play Russian roulette?”
Prior to the hearing, the day started with a press conference held on the steps of the Main Capitol Rotunda. Flick lead a message of equality for families where supporters held signs that read “Kids Need Both” and “House Bill 1499 Fairness for Families.”
“We are here for the kids,” Flick said. “We are here for Pennsylvania kids.”
Jeff Steiner, M.Ed., executive director of Dads’ Resource Center, offered stories of parents and grandparents who have been isolated from their children and grandchildren through unfair custody hearings. He said it’s frustrating for those who have been waiting since Rep. Flick introduced the bill on May 28, 2025, which he cited as 495 days, for something to happen.
“The support for House Bill 1499 demonstrates that shared parenting is not a partisan issue, because it’s about doing better for Pennsylvania children,” Steiner said. “Pennsylvanians overwhelmingly believe children should have the meaningful involvement of both parents following separation, and we now have an extraordinary bipartisan coalition of legislators willing to seriously examine how we can better serve these families.”
Robert Garza, director for Americans for Judicial Accountability and a nationally recognized advocate for children and parental rights, said he will continue urge parents to fight for 50/50 shared custody.
“This is about protecting the everyday moments that build relationships,” Garza said. “Moments no court can give back once they’re gone. I’m grateful to Rep. Flick for championing this effort.”
Mark Ludwig, executive director of the National Council for Equal Shared Parenting, spoke at the press conference. He has played a key role in advancing similar legislation in several states, including Kentucky, Arkansas, West Virginia, Florida and Missouri.
“Children should not lose a meaningful relationship with either parent simply because their parents no longer live together,” Ludwig said. “I’m proud to stand with Rep. Flick and Pennsylvania families in support of House Bill 1499. When both parents are willing, fit and able children deserve the opportunity to have both fully involved in their lives.”
Rael LaPenta, a member of Mothers Against Child Abuse, a national organization dedicated to protecting children from emotional, psychological, coercive and other forms of maltreatment, said the bill is in the best interest of parents and children.
“I’m a mother of both a son and a daughter,” LaPenta said. “This is not mothers versus fathers. It is about giving our children the safest, healthiest foundation possible. Pennsylvania has already done the studying and made the findings. Now we have the opportunity to act on them. I cannot look at my son and my daughter, and someday perhaps their children, and accept a system that still begins with assumptions instead of evidence. If we believe a child’s emotional and psychological well-being matters, and if Pennsylvania has already recognized the value of safe, meaningful relationships with both parents, then our custody laws should reflect it.”
Flick also took questions and listened to stories during a personal question-and-answer session where people from all over the Commonwealth shared their frustrations and hopes for reform.
“Pennsylvania can, and should, be a leader in child custody,” Flick said. “Without shared parenting, children are more likely to struggle in school, face emotional challenges and fall into cycles that hurt their future. I’m grateful for a day like this where we hear from families impacted by the corrupt child custody system, listen to experts who understand these issues and discuss how we can move this legislation forward to provide greater stability for children and families.”

title: Flick Announces Oct. 5 Press Conference, Hearing and Panel at State Capitol for Child Custody Reform Legislation
raw_text:
Flick Announces Oct. 5 Press Conference, Hearing and Panel at State Capitol for Child Custody Reform Legislation
September 28, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) today announced there will be a major day for his child custody reform legislation as there is a press conference, Judiciary Committee public hearing and panel all scheduled for Monday, Oct. 5, at the State Capitol in Harrisburg.
All the events will focus on
House Bill 1499
, authored by Flick, which would ensure fairness in custody determinations and protect the rights of children to have equal access to both parents, provided they are willing, able and fit.
“Momentum has been building for House Bill 1499,” Flick said. “I’m excited we’ve reached this point as I continue to hear from fathers, mothers and grandparents from across the country who share their own experiences about the need for reform. I encourage supporters of the legislation to come to Harrisburg if they can participate in this important day.”
A press conference will take place at 9 a.m. on the steps of the Main Capitol Rotunda. Speakers at the press conference will include Flick; Robert Garza, director for Americans for Judicial Accountability and a nationally recognized advocate for children and parental rights; Mark Ludwig, executive director of the National Council for Equal Shared Parenting; Jeff Steiner, M.Ed., executive director of Dads’ Resource Center; Hon. Mica Wood Pence, 43rd Circuit judge from Barren and Metcalfe counties in Kentucky, the first state to enact an equal parenting law; Hon. Tony Payton, former member, Pennsylvania House of Representatives; Teresa Sneed, founder, president and chief executive officer, National Family Justice; Rael LaPenta, a member of Mothers Against Child Abuse; and several other advocates of child custody reform.
“I am thrilled to have so many people who believe in the need for reform coming together at the Capitol,” Flick said. “House Bill 1499 has 78 co-sponsors from both parties and a grassroots petition that has gathered more than 2,800 signatures. This bill is really a child-focused bill as it considers the best interest of children when it comes to both safety and emotional wellbeing.”
Flick is also going to be part of a House Judiciary Committee public hearing at 10 a.m. in the Majority Caucus Room (140 Main Capitol) which will center on House Bill 1499.
“House Bill 1499 has been lingering in the Judiciary Committee since May 2025 despite having undeniable support,” Flick said. “This is a momentous opportunity to bring this issue before the committee.”
Flick will also be hosting a public House Bill 1499 Panel from 12:30 – 2 p.m. in Room B-31 Main Capitol. The panel will serve as an opportunity to hear directly from parents, grandparents and others who have been directly impacted by Pennsylvania’s current custody system within the framework of "why House Bill 1499 is important to me."
“I want to give as many people as possible the chance to be heard,” Flick said. “The panel will be a very public way to share the stories from parents who have lost access to their children at the whim of a judge or on a false allegation. My bill calls for 50/50 custody from the start for willing, able and fit parents, with a clear path for a modified custody agreement when clear and convincing evidence shows custody should not be 50/50.”
Pennsylvania has previously taken steps toward child custody reform. Last year, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed House Bill 378 into law as Act 11 of 2025. This bill reduces the factors a judge considers during child custody cases from 19 to 12. Flick wrote an amendment to the bill, which was unanimously passed by the House, requiring the court to give everyone a copy of the new factors within 30 days of modifications being made so that every party, including parents who often represent themselves because hiring lawyers is so expensive, has fair access to information.
“Act 11 of 2025 is working," Flick said. "In multiple cases, the Pennsylvania Superior Court has vacated and remanded lower court custody modifications because of a judge's failure to review the streamlined custody factors or provide written justifications in a timely manner as state law now mandates."
Flick was also a co-sponsor of  House Bill 414, now Act 40 of 2025, known as the Uniform Deployed Parents Custody and Visitation Act, which prohibits permanent custody changes during a parent’s military deployment. Shapiro signed the legislation into law at the end of October, which fixes a major flaw in the child custody system that allowed parents to use deployment as a reason to alter existing custody arrangements.
On Nov. 18, 2025 Flick also hosted another major day for shared parenting reform. A highlight from the day included a Republican Policy Committee hearing, where testifiers included Teresa Sneed, founder, president and chief executive officer, National Family Justice; Hon. Tony Payton, former member, Pennsylvania House of Representatives; Greg Fellerman, founding partner, Fellerman and Ciarimboli Law; and Hon. Mica Wood Pence.
Seven other states - Kentucky, Arkansas, West Virginia, Florida, Missouri, Louisiana and Mississippi - have passed or adopted similar child custody legislation.
“Pennsylvania can, and should, be a leader in child custody,” Flick said. “Without shared parenting, children are more likely to struggle in school, face emotional challenges and fall into cycles that hurt their future.”
Flick welcomes all who are able to attend the events on Oct. 5. For those who can’t attend, he will be streaming the events on his Facebook page and his website, www.RepFlick.com.

title: Looking Back on the 79th Little League World Series
raw_text:
Looking Back on the 79th Little League World Series
September 2, 2026
by State Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union)
Now that the Little League World Series (LLWS) has come and gone I wanted to take a moment to recognize some of the special moments. We can agree that some of the highlights this year include Curaçao’s pitching domination in the final game, Japan’s heartfelt celebration after winning their final matchup with help from their smallest player. There was also the record-setting play of both “girls with game,” Kinley Rasmus of Phenix City, Alabama, and Carsynn Meyer of Paseo Verde Little League in Las Vegas, Nevada.
One of my favorite moments of the series didn’t even occur on the diamond, but on the slick, muddy hill. I watched the kids slide down, run back up, and slide back down; a frenzy of kids caked in mud having fun. But when the speakers began to play a national anthem, whether it was the Star-Spangled Banner or another country’s anthem, they stopped in deference to the tradition. I was proud to witness such respect, and it affirms that, yes, the kids are alright.
This year I volunteered as Team Host for Team Canada, and I saw and experienced kindness, respect, great sportsmanship, and commendable behavior in the Canadians and all the teams who came to play on our fields. I’m left feeling encouraged and hopeful.
I also want to congratulate the brave and determined players of the Challenger Exhibition game held on Saturday. It is possibly the most joyful game of the Series, when the kids who face physical and developmental challenges take to the field, swing the bat and run the bases. This year’s teams hailed from Berwyn/Paoli, Pennsylvania, and Oakley, California. Before the players met at Volunteer Stadium, they practiced at the Original Little League Field in Williamsport, and they participated in a program called Drums Alive with the Superstars group at the Williamsport YMCA. Many thanks to the Superstars, the Williamsport YMCA, BLaST IU17, Park Pizza for donating pizzas to both teams, PepsiCo, and especially the families for supporting their kids on the long journey to Williamsport.
Lastly, I want to take a moment to congratulate all of us, as fans and as hosts. The Little League World Series is our time to show the world that North Central Pennsylvania, the 83rd District, South Williamsport, Williamsport, and the surrounding communities are great places to live, populated with good and welcoming people. I believe we rose to that occasion yet again. Thank you for collectively coming together to make the 79th Little League World Series a success.

House Adopts Flick’s Resolution Recognizing Little League World Series Week
June 30, 2026
HARRISBURG – Recognizing its cherished tradition and the significant impact it has on the Commonwealth, Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) announced Aug. 19-30, 2026, will be recognized as “Little League World Series Week” in Pennsylvania. The designation follows the successful passage of a resolution he sponsored, which was approved by an overwhelming majority in the House of Representatives.
House Resolution 554
honors the Little League World Series, which is held each year in South Williamsport, the birthplace of Little League. It also recognizes Carl E. Stotz, who founded Little League in 1939.
“I’m proud to pay tribute to Carl, whose vision and dedication gave rise to Little League and helped shape generations of young athletes,” Flick said. “This resolution is an opportunity to celebrate the value of teamwork, sportsmanship and community that continue to define the Little League World Series and our region.”
Each year tens of thousands of visitors from around the world travel to South Williamsport for the Little League World Series. It’s estimated the event bring in $40 million to the economy as teams from Canada to Cuba, Texas to Taiwan, and Pennsylvania to Puerto Rico compete to become world champions.
Flick, who has not missed a Little League World Series tournament for more than 50 years, serves as a team host and hosts an annual picnic for two of the participating teams.
“This resolution ensures we continue to honor the history and values Little League represents,” Flick said. “I’m looking forward to this year’s World Series and to welcoming the young athletes and families who make this event so special.”
In speaking on the House floor in support of his resolution, Flick paid tribute to Karen Stotz Myers, the daughter of Stotz, who remains an active advocate for preserving and recognizing the league’s original field about five miles from where the World Series is played today. He also recognized Billy Martin of Houston, Texas., who threw the first no-hitter in the 1950 Little League World Series and continues to return to the tournament.

title: Decision Shaped by Open Debate and Informed Discussions, Not Party Lines
raw_text:
Decision Shaped by Open Debate and Informed Discussions, Not Party Lines
June 2, 2026
by State Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union)
Laws are created for many reasons: for protection, regulation, to promote fairness and safety, establish consistency, resolve conflicts, and enable trust. When legislators vote, we are responsible for educating ourselves and being open to hearing both sides of an issue.
At times, I can vote on a bill with firm conviction. Other times I listen to arguments for and against and find myself changing my mind with each new speaker. What will be best for everyone in the long run? This was the case with House Bill 1814, which passed in the House on June 1.
House Bill 1814
would ban the possession and use of cell phones and other mobile devices by students in K–12 during school hours in both public and private learning environments across the Commonwealth, with certain exemptions included in the legislation.
My instinct was to vote ‘yes.’ I believe cell phone use is hindering education in classrooms, with students of all ages distracted by whatever content is more interesting than the subject at hand. As a grown adult, I find myself distracted, drawn to my phone to learn, to be entertained or to follow whatever discussion is taking over social media. My initial “yes” was based on the belief that it would take a law to rein in cell phone usage in schools.
Then I thought about my belief in small government, and not making sweeping laws to govern every inch of this diverse Commonwealth with one stroke of a pen. School districts elect people to make policies that fit their educational needs, isn’t that the role of a school board? My vote then swung to “no.”
Then I thought about how local elections can sometimes go awry if the candidates elected are not qualified or willing to listen to and act on the best interest of their constituents. I think of Muncy Township and the swelling discontent with the chairperson of that board of supervisors. Is it sometimes better to pass laws to govern from the top? Maybe I should vote “yes.”
I listened to the arguments made in the House chamber, both for and against, and then I made some phone calls to local superintendents and to a handful of school board presidents. We talked about the issue.
Around 420 of 500 school districts in the Commonwealth already have a cell phone policy in place. Here in the 83rd District, schools have differing policies that seem to be working well for them. Making these decisions is what local elected officials, school board directors, are elected to do. I voted “no.”
House Bill 1814 does not resolve all conflicts, build trust or promote fairness regarding the autonomy school districts need to meet the needs of students, teachers and administrators.
The House ultimately passed the bill by a vote of 126 to 75. Support and opposition to the bill came from both parties. This was not a vote divided by party, but by educated differences of opinion, and that’s how it is supposed to work.
House Bill 1814 now heads to the Senate, which has already passed a similar bill. Senate members will consider the amendments the House made to the bill before making their final vote.

title: House Approves Flick’s Resolution Honoring Negro Leagues

House Approves Flick’s Resolution Honoring Negro Leagues
May 4, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) announced May 2, 2026, is now Negro Leagues Day in Pennsylvania. The designation follows the successful passage of a resolution he sponsored, which was approved on Monday by an overwhelming majority in the House of Representatives.
House Resolution 481
recognizes the contributions African American baseball players made to the game and acknowledges the significant impact the Negro Leagues had on the civil rights movement nationwide.
“In 1865, one of the first Negro baseball clubs was formed in Philadelphia, the Philadelphia Phythians,” Flick said. “For over a century and a half, Pennsylvania has been a shining example of how sports, specifically baseball, can be a place of inclusion. This resolution ensures that legacy is honored and the stories of these groundbreaking players continue to be shared.”
Flick, an avid baseball fan, belongs to the Williamsport chapter of the Society for American Baseball Research (SABR). This chapter is known as the George Stovey chapter. Stovey, who was born and lived in Williamsport, is widely recognized as one of the best left-handed pitchers of the 19th century, but unfortunately, because of the color of his skin, he was not allowed to play in the major leagues.
Flick credits SABR members in the Williamsport, Harrisburg and Philadelphia chapters for suggesting the idea of the resolution. He said he wants to ensure players like Stovey receive the recognition they were long denied.
“Baseball is America’s pastime, and I think it’s past time George Stovey and great players like him are recognized,” Flick said. “Without proper recognition, Stovey and so many players like him have been left out of the Baseball Hall of Fame.”

Flick's Fourth Speaker Series and Human Services Expo Highlights Community Resources and Opioid Awareness
April 24, 2026
WILLIAMSPORT
– On Thursday, April 23, Rep. Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union) hosted his fourth annual Speaker Series and Human Services Expo at the Pennsylvania College of Technology. The events served as opportunities to explore services and hear from voices working on the challenges communities face.
The topic of this year’s speaker series was Opioid Addiction: Loss, Recovery and Hope. It featured a powerful lineup of speakers who addressed the challenges communities continue to face and the progress being made. Speakers included Reps. Doyle Heffley (R-Carbon) and Dan Williams (D-Chester), chairs of the House Human Services Committee; Carolyn Miele, founder of Saving Lives for Zachary; Marc Lovecchio, an attorney and former Lycoming County judge; Kevin McNamara, a father who lost his son to an overdose; Kydreece Burks, an alumni of Williamsport Area High School and current senior at Penn State University; and Jennier Reeder, assistant director of West Branch Drug and Alcohol Abuse Commission.
Throughout all of the presentations, a consistent message emerged: the devastating impact of opioids on individuals and families, and the importance of remembering the humanity of those impacted.
“These were very raw and real stories that were shared,” Flick said. “I am grateful for their willingness to speak openly, as it helps reduce stigma and brings hope to families who are still struggling.”
Marc Lovecchio, an attorney and former Lycoming County judge, talked about how he lost his younger brother, David, to addiction and how that experience continues to shape his work and advocacy.
“Substance use disorder is an equal opportunity killer,” Lovecchio said. “I grew up in a nice family; there were six of us. When my brother was at his worst, or lowest, he ruined my family. It’s taken me 15 years to be able to cope with the guilt that I thought I had control over it. I still have a lot of hope. There is treatment out there, education is important.”
Carolyn Miele, who has been outspoken about the death of her son, Zachary, in 2016, told the audience her son’s story took a tragic turn when he started using marijuana. Miele said that experience led her to start her nonprofit named after her son to reduce the stigma surrounding substance use disorder and to help families recognize the early warning signs before addiction takes hold.
“There were a lot of people who had lost their children at the same time I lost Zachary,” Miele said. “I hate to see other families go through what I’ve gone through. Substance abuse thrives in silence and misunderstanding, but it loses its power when communities come together with knowledge and compassion.”
Jennifer Reeder, assistant director at West Branch Drug and Alcohol, ended the Speaker Series by providing an update on the number of overdoses in Lycoming County. She said the county has seen a 62% drop in overdose deaths over the past year.
Reeder also provided an overview for the services her agency provides.
“We’re looking at all the hurdles that prevent people getting engaged with recovery,” Reeder said. “We want to make sure we ease that process as much as we can.”
The Human Services Expo featured around 70 vendors offering a wide range of community resources, connecting attendees to services related to aging, autism, behavioral health, career development, children and adolescents, diverse physical and intellectual abilities, early intervention, housing and transportation, independent living, medical assistance, mental health, substance abuse, veterans’ services and more.
“Families tell me every day how overwhelming it can be to track down services,” Flick said. “As a member of the House Human Services Committee, I’m glad to see this expo can make that process simpler by bringing so many essential resources together for the community.”
New to the Expo this year were the Williamsport Police Department; Technology for our Whole Lives (TechOWL); PPL Electric Utilities’ Wrap Program; Dad's Resource Center and resources on custody; and United Churches of Lycoming County.
American Rescue Workers (ARW) has participated in the expo each year it has taken place.
The nonprofit provides homelessness and hunger prevention services in Lycoming County.
Jennifer Rempe, director of Development and Community Engagement at ARW, said the organization finds a lot of value in the expo.
“It’s great for us to get out and be in the public,” Rempe said. “We can really get the word out about the food component along with the social services part. We can also network with all the other vendors, which helps us support each other’s work.”
Students from Pennsylvania College of Technology’s Physician Assistant Program offered complimentary blood pressure screenings. Staff from the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, along with students and staff from Penn College’s Information Technology Program, provided information about cybersecurity and scams.
Todd Burke, from Catawissa, came to the expo looking to connect with information about drug and alcohol awareness.
“I think it’s great to have the variety of different resources,” Burke said. “You can go from table to table and talk to people, and based on your family’s needs, get the resources you need.”

“Opioids have affected nearly everyone in some way,” Flick said. “Whether you, a friend, a son or daughter, spouse or relative have struggled with addiction, or sadly lost a friend or loved one, you will find something to connect with.”
The discussion will start with House Human Services committee chairs, Rep. Dan Williams (D-Chester) and Rep. Doyle Heffley (R-Carbon). The chairmen will provide an update on the committee and legislation being worked on at the Capitol.
“As a member of the Human Services Committee, I’m honored Rep. Williams and Rep. Heffley will share their perspectives on this critical issue and provide updates from Harrisburg.”
A panel of four individuals whose lives have been forever altered by opioids will share their stories, including Carolyn Miele, founder of Saving Lives for Zachary; Marc Lovecchio, an attorney and former Lycoming County judge; Kevin McNamara, father who lost his son to overdose; and Kydreece Burks, alumni of Williamsport Area High School and current senior at Penn State University.
“The stories reveal the tragic consequences of opioids, and serve as part cautionary tale, part resilience and part hope for an addiction-free future,” Flick said.
Flick will close the Speaker Series with updated information about the Pennsylvania Opioid Misuse and Addiction Abatement Trust, and the strides the Commonwealth, and the area, are making against the epidemic of opioid addiction.
The Speaker Series is free to the public.
Immediately following the Speaker Series, the Human Services Expo will take place at the Field House on the Pennsylvania College of Technology campus from 3-6 p.m. The Expo is also free and open to the public and will offer valuable information and resources for the community from more than 70 agencies, businesses and nonprofits.

title: Flick Named ‘Champion for Children’ by National Organization

Flick Named ‘Champion for Children’ by National Organization
October 15, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Jamie Flick (R Lycoming/Union) has been named an inaugural recipient of the Champion for Children Award by the National Parents Organization (NPO).
The national honor recognizes legislative and judicial leaders who champion legal defaults that protect a child's fundamental right to maintain meaningful, loving relationships with both fit parents after separation.
“This recognition is truly humbling,” Flick said. “NPO is a respected national leader in advancing family court reform that puts children first. I am so very grateful to receive this award as I have fought for years to modernize our family court system and ensure that children remain at the center of every decision.”
Flick has gained recognition across the country for his work on his
House Bill 1499
, which seeks to ensure fairness in custody determinations and protect children’s rights to have equal access to both parents, provided they are willing, fit and able.
Flick was presented with the Champion for Children Award by Don Hubin, Ph.D., National Board Chair of NPO at a press conference he hosted at the State Capitol during a day on which House Bill 1499 was the focus of the conference, a Judiciary Committee public hearing and panel.
“Rep. Flick has demonstrated extraordinary courage and conviction in confronting the outdated defaults of our family court system," said Hubin. "Where many see an immovable judicial status quo, Rep. Flick sees an urgent moral obligation to protect children. His sponsorship of House Bill 1499 and his tireless leadership of the 'Kids Need Both' initiative reflect an unwavering commitment to making equal shared parenting the standard in Pennsylvania. Social science consistently shows that children thrive when both parents remain fully engaged in their lives, and Rep. Flick’s visionary legislative work is laying the foundation for stronger, healthier families across the Commonwealth."
In addition to his work on House Bill 1499, Flick also successfully amended
House Bill 378
, now Act 11 of 2025. The law reduces the factors a judge considers during child custody cases from 19 to 12. Flick’s amendment required the court to give everyone a copy of the new factors within 30 days of modifications being made so that every party, including parents who often represent themselves because hiring lawyers is so expensive, has fair access to information.
Flick, who is also a father of six and a Court Appointed Special Advocate (CASA) for foster youth, was named a co-recipient of the Champion for Children Award with the Hon. Mica Wood Pence, 43rd Circuit judge from Barren and Metcalfe counties in Kentucky.
